title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Language Model Training Dynamics

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states that only “selected pre-trained and post-trained models,” “portions” of datasets, and “partial evaluation scripts” will be released, and that “full training pipelines and all data cannot be fully released.” In contrast, the Introduction claims “Open-sourcing 100+ LMs ... and their training data for all stages” and “a comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible training pipeline and evaluation framework.” These are materially incompatible release and reproducibility claims.

The text repeatedly relies on “Table 1” for central quantitative claims, including the claimed comparison of 1B-320BT and 4B-80BT models and the claim that Maj@16 can underperform greedy before RL. No Table 1 appears anywhere in the supplied paper. Consequently, the cited numerical evidence is unavailable and cannot support the associated conclusions.

Section 2.1 says pretraining begins at “20× model size (compute-optimal).” For a 4B model, that lower bound is 80B tokens. But Section 3.1 and the Figure 1 caption describe experiments on “{0.5B, 1B, 4B}-{10BT, 20BT, 40BT, 80BT, 160BT, 320BT},” which implies 4B runs at 10B, 20B, and 40B tokens, below 20×. The appendix only reports 4B results from 80B onward. The experimental grid is therefore inconsistently described.

The paper calls 8B FineWeb replay plus 42B FineMath “around 5%” replay. The replay fraction is 8/(8+42)=16%, or 8/42=19% if expressed relative to FineMath tokens; neither is approximately 5%. The stated quantitative interpretation of the purported optimum is arithmetically false.

Takeaway 3 says domain-specific CPT “could harm both upstream and downstream performance.” The only downstream numbers in Table 2 show every CPT condition substantially outperforming no CPT on GSM8K-Platinum (No CPT 6.04%; pure FineMath 19.27%; replay variants 15.22–21.01%). The reported table supports upstream forgetting and differences among replay mixes, but does not support a claim that CPT harmed downstream performance relative to the no-CPT baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4, Figure 7(b) caption and accompanying text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says the RL dataset-size experiment uses “a fixed epoch of 8,” and Appendix A.2 refers to the 400K-example run as “400Kep8.” However, Figure 7(b)'s model specification says “{0, 50K, 100K, 150K, ..., 400K}-ep1.” Since conclusions about the effect of dataset size depend critically on the number of RL epochs, the caption and text describe different experiments.

The paper attributes RL collapse to generations “often exceed[ing] their predefined context-window lengths.” Yet Table 5 specifies a 2,048-token context window, while Table 8 specifies max_prompt_length=1,024 and max_response_length=1,024. Under the stated implementation, prompt plus response is capped at 2,048 tokens and cannot exceed the stated context limit. Either the actual training settings differed from Table 8 or the proposed explanation for the collapse is impossible as written.

The body reports that greedy, Maj@16, and RM@16 peak around 8–16 RL epochs and that dataset-size gains continue to roughly 150–200K examples. Takeaway 9 instead says saturation occurs at “4–8 epochs or 50–100K examples.” The latter is inconsistent with the ranges stated immediately above it; additionally, the text says Pass@16 degrades beyond 4 epochs, so it cannot generally be summarized as excessive RL improving downstream performance.

Figures 5 and 6 are not usable plots of the claimed experiments. They contain apparent axis/tick fragments and repeated sequences (for example, Figure 5 lists only “4 8 16 32” under an experiment stated to use {1,2,4,8,16,32}; Figure 6 lists “100 200 300 400” despite a stated 50K–400K sweep). No model-performance curves or numerical observations are shown. The conclusions in Section 3.3 therefore cannot be checked against the figures claimed to establish them.

The paper calls [56] “LLaMA-2” in Section 2.1 and uses it for Llama 3.2 in Table 4. Reference [56] is Touvron et al., “LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models” (the original LLaMA paper), not the Llama 2 paper and not a Llama 3.2 technical report. These attributions should be corrected.
FineMath is cited as “FineMath [38],” but [38] is the FineWeb dataset paper. The paper’s own reference list identifies the FineMath/SmolLM2 source as [2]. This is a direct incorrect citation.

Appendix B.3.2 says it provides standard errors from four random-seed experiments and introduces “Table 9: Standard errors of main results,” but no Table 9 values appear. Thus the claimed uncertainty quantification is absent, despite the main text making saturation and degradation claims that require it.

The purported GSM8K-Platinum example is a concatenation of unrelated benchmark prompts and outputs: it begins with a BoardgameQA-style animal-rule problem, contains an instruction requiring a True/False/Uncertain answer, then includes a CRUXEval Python-function prompt and its answer, then a GSM8K-style Bali-change problem and its answer, before resuming the boardgame prompt. This cannot be a valid single input-output evaluation example and indicates corrupted prompt assembly, erroneous labeling, or contaminated reporting.

The paper calls ORM score a “reliable unsupervised proxy metric” and suggests it can validate models without labeled evaluations based only on correlations among related post-training variants sharing the same 1B base model and training pipeline. The ORM itself is a supervised reward model, and correlations across non-independent variants do not establish reliability, out-of-family generalization, or an unsupervised validation capability. The evidence supports at most an in-family association, not the broad proposed use.
